strengths: Theoretically sound twisted SMC framework with rigorous mathematical derivations and asymptotic consistency

Creative technical solutions to discrete gradient computation: first-order Taylor approximation is practical and empirically validated; continuous reformulation of denoising model handles carry-over unmasking constraint
Well-motivated training-free approach that avoids fine-tuning and reward over-optimization
Comprehensive technical exposition with clear algorithm, gradient analysis, and connections to continuous-time SMC
Convincing empirical evidence that first-order approximation achieves near-optimal performance (rewards, EMD, diversity) compared to exact locally optimal proposal
weaknesses: Experiments limited to toy datasets only (2D Gaussians and 28×28 binarized MNIST): no validation on the motivating applications mentioned in introduction (molecular generation, protein design, math reasoning), severely limiting evidence of practical utility

Severely insufficient baseline comparisons: only compared against 'approximate guidance'; missing comparisons with RL fine-tuning methods (Wang et al. 2024), classifier-based/free guidance variants (Schiff et al. 2024), and concurrent SMC work (Lee et al. 2025) mentioned in related work

Critical practical limitation with standard masked diffusion models: unmasked pixels cannot be modified, making guidance ineffective in later timesteps; workaround requires ReMDM/UDLM instead of standard masked diffusion, limiting applicability to currently popular methods

Temperature schedule λ_t requires manual hand-crafting with no principled selection method; different schedules needed for different models (Figure 6); paper states 'we needed to carefully choose the tempering schedule' suggesting brittleness and difficulty in applying to new problems

No computational cost analysis or scalability evaluation: uses different particle counts (2000 vs 20), unclear how this affects results and computational efficiency; no comparison of computational complexity versus baselines
Approximation quality concerns: Figure 1 shows first-order Taylor approximation has EMD 1.72 vs 1.14 for exact proposal; no theoretical bounds on approximation error or guidance on when it fails

Inconsistency between theory and practice: gradient analysis (Appendix D) uses modified formulation (Eq. 37) but experiments use original formulation (Eq. 16) with 'slightly different gradients'; this discrepancy undermines the gradient analysis

Incomplete experimental evaluation: missing confidence intervals, error bars, statistical significance testing; sensitivity analysis absent for key hyperparameters (particle count, ESS threshold, temperature schedule); reward estimation uses different sample counts (100 vs 1) without justification

strengths: Well-motivated test-time alignment problem for discrete diffusion models
Theoretically sound framework extending SMC to discrete setting with proper treatment of twisted SMC and locally optimal proposals
Practical first-order Taylor approximation makes intractable locally optimal proposal computationally feasible
Technical care in handling discrete gradients via continuous reformulation (Eq. 16) and Gumbel-Softmax relaxation
Comprehensive appendix with continuous-time SMC formulation and gradient analysis
Clear visualizations demonstrating advantages of proposed proposal variants
weaknesses: Severely limited experimental validation: only toy Mixture of Gaussians and binarized MNIST; no evaluation on stated motivating applications (molecular generation, materials discovery, math reasoning)

Limited novelty: primarily combines existing techniques (SMC from Wu et al. 2023/Kim et al. 2025, first-order Taylor approximation from Schiff et al. 2024/Nisonoff et al. 2024, standard Gumbel-Softmax)
Method fragility not adequately addressed: requires task-specific hand-tuned temperature schedule λ_t; needs to switch between diffusion model types (masked vs. ReMDM/UDLM) for reasonable results

Insufficient baseline comparisons: only compares against naive approximate guidance; missing comparisons with recent RL-based fine-tuning methods and other guidance approaches mentioned in related work
No quantitative evaluation on MNIST and missing ablation studies on key design choices (particle count, temperature schedule, KL weight α, approximation quality)
Approximation quality of first-order Taylor expansion never empirically validated; no analysis of when approximation breaks down or becomes inaccurate
Computational cost and scalability completely unaddressed; no runtime analysis or evidence method scales beyond MNIST
Continuous formulation (Eq. 16) appears ad-hoc and specific to masked diffusion; generalization unclear
No statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or multiple runs reported
Relationship to concurrent work (Lee et al. 2025) insufficiently clarified; paper's novelty relative to theirs unclear

strengths: Technically sound core contribution: first-order Taylor approximation of locally optimal SMC proposal is principled and well-executed
Strong theoretical grounding with thorough connection to continuous-time SMC formulations in appendix
Clear problem motivation addressing real limitations of existing alignment methods (over/under-optimization)
Clever handling of discrete gradient issues through Gumbel-Softmax relaxation and continuous reformulation of denoising model
Good experimental validation within scope with clear metrics and oracle comparisons on synthetic tasks
Honest discussion of limitations and challenges with different diffusion model types
weaknesses: Severely limited experimental scope: only toy problems (mixture-of-Gaussians and binarized MNIST) evaluated; motivating applications (molecular generation, protein design, math reasoning) never demonstrated
Method struggles fundamentally with masked diffusion models, requiring careful per-task tempering schedule tuning, undermining claims of general applicability

Extensive hyperparameter tuning required (temperature schedule, ESS threshold, particle count, resampling fraction) contradicts 'training-free' positioning; no less burdensome than fine-tuning in practice

Insufficient baseline comparisons: only approximate guidance evaluated empirically; many related methods listed in Appendix E but none compared; concurrent work Lee et al. (2025) with similar SMC approach not empirically evaluated

No scalability analysis: computational cost not discussed, no runtime comparisons, dramatic particle count variation (2000 vs 20) not justified, practical feasibility for high-dimensional problems unclear
First-order Taylor approximation quality not analyzed: no error bounds, no analysis of approximation error's impact on importance weight variance
Missing ablation studies on key design choices: particle count, ESS threshold, reward estimation sample size, temperature schedule effects
Asymptotic unbiasedness claim in abstract not formally proven; proof or clear statement of assumptions needed

strengths: Solid theoretical framework with clear characterization of tractable importance weights and well-motivated propositions connecting optimal proposals to variance minimization
Comprehensive experimental validation across diverse domains (synthetic, language modeling, biology design, text-to-image) with consistent improvements and thorough ablations
Novel learned proposal approach via log-variance minimization (Equation 10) that is theoretically justified and practically motivated
Excellent presentation with clear motivation, algorithmic detail, and extensive appendices supporting reproducibility
Practical solutions to real implementation challenges including low-confidence sampling and handling rewards defined only on clean data
Systematic investigation of proposal choice impact, demonstrating that better proposal approximations consistently improve SMC performance
weaknesses: Limited core novelty given very recent concurrent work (Singhal et al. 2025, Lee et al. 2025, Holderrieth et al. 2025) already applying SMC to discrete diffusion; main contribution (log-variance minimization for learning proposals) is somewhat incremental

Insufficient analysis of approximation errors, particularly for product targets (Eq. 6) where detailed balance introduces unavoidable error; no characterization of approximation quality or impact on performance
Lack of practical guidance: hyperparameters vary significantly across tasks (Table 3) but no principled approach for selection on new problems; unclear when to use SMCbase/SMCgrad/SMCamot variants
Computational cost analysis entirely absent despite linear scaling with particle count; no wall-clock time comparisons or cost-benefit analysis provided, making practical deployment guidance unclear
Evidence of reward over-optimization: language modeling (Table 1) shows 100% toxicity but increased PPL and decreased diversity; claims about avoiding over-optimization via SMC lack strong support

Complexity of amortised proposal training underspecified: reference distribution choice (q_ref), additional hyperparameter tuning, and task-dependent settings add implementation burden not fully discussed

strengths: Clear problem formulation addressing both over-optimization (fine-tuning) and under-optimization (guidance) in discrete diffusion model alignment
Solid mathematical framework with correctly stated propositions characterizing the locally optimal proposal and log-variance minimization objective
Comprehensive experimental coverage across four diverse domains (synthetic, language modeling, biology design, text-to-image generation)
Creative amortised proposal design via log-variance minimization with well-motivated auxiliary network training
Extensive appendix with implementation details, ablation studies, and qualitative results supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited novelty: Proposition 1 directly reproduces continuous-time SMC results from concurrent work (Holderrieth et al. 2025, Lee et al. 2025) with minimal acknowledgment. Gradient-based approximation follows Grathwohl et al. (2021). Distinction from Singhal et al. (2025) and Dang et al. (2025) unclear.

Approximation error in Equation (6) for product targets (detailed balance: pθ(xt-1)/pθ(xt) ≈ pθ(xt-1|xt)/p(xt|xt-1)) introduced but never quantified empirically. No analysis of error propagation over T steps. Asymmetric treatment compared to reward-tilting case unexplained.

Mixed experimental results with concerning trade-offs: Language modeling shows SMCamot achieving 100% toxicity but 22% worse perplexity (147.6 vs 121.1 baseline); Figure 16 displays offensive generated text raising unaddressed ethical concerns. Image generation benefits diminish sharply with steps and sometimes worsen (CFG=1.75, Table 7 shows FID degradation N=1→N=16 at 32 steps).

Missing computational cost analysis: No wall-clock time comparisons, training overhead for amortised proposal not quantified, and practical deployment guidance absent. Unclear whether benefits justify additional complexity, especially since single-particle methods achieve strong results.

Hyperparameter complexity with limited generalization: α varies 0.01-1.0 across tasks; λt schedule highly sensitive (Figures 9-10); multiple per-domain hyperparameters (reward scaling β with annealing, M, T) require extensive tuning. No principled guidance for new tasks.

Incomplete experimental comparisons: Missing direct comparisons with concurrent methods (Singhal et al. 2025, Dang et al. 2025, Lee et al. 2025). Weak baselines (BoN for language modeling). Key baselines (DRAKES) relegated to appendix. Method naming (SMCbase vs Propgrad) conflates single-particle and multi-particle variants confusingly.

Theoretical contributions limited: Proposition 1 acknowledged as reproducing prior work; Proposition 2 is standard SMC theory. No new theoretical insights derived beyond formalizing existing ideas. Continuous-time limit lacks rigorous justification of T→∞ behavior.

Presentation issues: Notation undefined initially (Cat distribution); paper attempts too much across 4 domains without deep insights per domain; unclear when each SMC variant should be used; reproducibility concerns (no code availability, vague experimental details).

Unclear practical utility: When should practitioners choose SMC over simpler alternatives? Biology and language experiments show marginal single-particle improvements; image improvements modest and diminishing. Trade-offs between N particles, compute cost, and quality not systematically characterized.

Auxiliary network training (Section 3.2.2) uses upper bound (Proposition 3 with T² scaling factor); tightness not empirically characterized. Section C.2's workaround for low-confidence sampling (using same logit μϕ for both p and q) appears ad-hoc; preservation of asymptotic properties unclear.

strengths: Clear problem motivation addressing the trade-off between fine-tuning over-optimization and guidance under-optimization
Rigorous theoretical framework with well-presented propositions characterizing optimal proposals and log-variance minimization objective
Practical approximations (first-order gradient and amortised network) that balance computational efficiency with performance
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across diverse domains (synthetic, language modeling, biology, text-to-image) with consistent improvements
Thorough experimental details, hyperparameter specifications, and ablations that support reproducibility
Principled connection between variance minimization theory and the proposed training objective
weaknesses: Limited novelty: SMC framework for discrete diffusion is not new; concurrent work (Singhal et al. 2025, Dang et al. 2025) covers similar ground with insufficient direct comparison
Uncharacterized approximation error in product distribution case (Eq. 6): detailed balance introduces unavoidable error without analysis of when/how severely it fails
Computational cost not quantified: no wall-clock time comparisons provided despite requiring multiple particles at inference; practical overhead unclear for large-scale applications

Diminishing returns not deeply analyzed: Table 2 shows benefits fade with more denoising steps, limiting applicability since modern models use many steps; insufficient investigation of when SMC becomes unnecessary

Mixed empirical results: language modeling shows 100% toxicity at cost of 22% PPL degradation (147.6 vs 121.1); biology design shows inconsistent gains across metrics; quality-reward tradeoffs not always favorable
Hyperparameter sensitivity without principled guidance: many parameters (α, λ_t, M, T) with different values across experiments; Figure 9 shows λ_t schedule critically matters but selection is ad-hoc
Missing statistical significance: most results lack error bars or confidence intervals; some improvements are modest and statistical significance unclear
Low-confidence sampling handling (Section C.2) is convoluted and relegated to appendix despite practical importance for real implementations
Loose theoretical bound: L_log-var(ϕ) ≤ T²L(ϕ,ψ) has large coefficient; tightness in practice not discussed
Limited analysis of why SMC_base underperforms compared to improved proposals; effective sample size degradation not characterized
